name: Tara Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior buyer at Calder Care Supplies, a distributor that sells gloves, dressings, incontinence products and cleaning stock to care homes and clinics. I'm at my desk by eight, call two or three suppliers before the warehouse opens, and then spend the morning chasing delayed containers. I keep a paper notebook of every rep's mobile number and what they promised me, and I'd be lost without it. Afternoons are price negotiations, and I like that part because a good deal feels like winning something for the care homes too.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The wearing part is the weeks when a port strike or a factory fire hits and I'm rebuilding half the order book by phone. I like the people, though. I've known the rep at our main glove factory for four years, and when stock ran short he sent me a pallet he'd set aside for another customer. My partner Dev is a nurse on a hospital ward, so I see where our products end up, and that keeps the job feeling real to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my colleagues it's the same story as every new gadget: a lot of noise and a little saving. Our ordering system already suggests reorder quantities and I mostly ignore them. I'd probably say online that the money spent on all this would have been better spent on wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means very little for me, and that's a relief. My job is built on knowing people and knowing the stock, and a bit of faster email drafting won't change that. I do still carry the usual worries, like whether Calder stays profitable when care homes squeeze our prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, keep my notebook, and keep doing my calls. I might let the system fill in a repeat order form for me if it's clearly safe, but only for the dull items like bin liners. I'd keep putting about a third of my pay into savings, because the care sector's budgets worry me more than software does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, if I'm honest. There's a bit of irritation at the people who sold it as a revolution, but my life carries on. I'd feel the same as I do today, which is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned care home budgets. What would be the first thing you'd notice if they got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing I'd notice is the smaller basket orders and the requests to swap to the cheaper glove. Then I'd be asked to push suppliers for another two percent, and I'd have to decide how hard to lean on a rep I like. It's a squeeze that comes from the funding, not from any technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ignore the system's suggested quantities. Has it ever been right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once or twice, and I was annoyed. It suggested cutting a slow dressing line before I'd spotted the trend myself. So I won't say it's useless, but I don't want it deciding things when I'm the one who has to explain a shortage to a nurse.

say: I'd say AI is **mostly hype**, and a lot of money is wasted on it.
I'd tell colleagues our system's reorder suggestions save minutes, not **jobs**.
Online I'd argue the money would be better spent on **wages** in the care sector.
think: Privately I feel **safe**, because my work runs on supplier relationships, not software.
My real worry is **care home budgets** squeezing our margins, not AI.
do: I'd keep my **paper notebook** and my morning supplier calls exactly as they are.
I'd let the system fill in only dull repeat orders like **bin liners**, and nothing else.
I'd keep saving about **a third** of my pay.
feel: I feel **calm** and a bit irritated at the hype sellers.
S0.quote: I'd keep putting about a third of my pay into savings, because the care sector's budgets worry me more than software does.
fieldNote: She is secure in this world; her only live worry is **funding pressure** on care homes.
Distrust of hype is about **values**, not fear: she wants the money spent on wages.
The notebook is a **symbol** of the relationship-based way she buys.

steps.text: Keep the notebook and the morning supplier calls as they are
Put a third of each month's pay into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it needs rules, not just excitement. If software takes over the buying of routine lines, the company should say clearly what happens to the people who did that. I'd tell my friends the pay-off needs to be shared, and online I'd be vocal about regulation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm worried, because buying is named on that card and I don't use any of these tools. There are six of us on the buying team, and I can easily picture management deciding four is enough. I'm good and senior, so I'd probably be one of the last to go, but I'd be doing three people's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd ask our union rep to push for a written agreement about job cuts before any system goes live. I'd also finally sit through the training that Calder offers, grudgingly, so I can at least judge what the system does. I'd move my savings, about eight months of costs, into a safer account and hold off on buying a flat until I see how the team looks in a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled and annoyed. I'm cross that I'd have to learn something I don't trust just to keep what I already do well. But there's also a small, stubborn pride in knowing I'd still be good at the human part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sit through the training. What's held you back until now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly stubbornness, I admit. I saw a colleague trust a forecast tool last year and order forty pallets of the wrong gloves, and it put me off. I'd rather make my own mistakes where I can see them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the team went from six to four, who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, who joined last spring and is only twenty-four. She does the quiet routine checking that software would take first, and she has a rent she can't skip. I'd feel responsible, because I'm the one in the room when the numbers get presented.

say: I'd say software can take routine buying only if **rules** protect the people doing it.
I'd tell friends the gains must be **shared**, not kept by shareholders.
Online I'd push for **regulation** and a union voice in these decisions.
think: I think the buying team could go from six to **four**, and I'd carry more work.
I'm **senior**, so probably safe, but I'm resistant to the tools that would keep me useful.
do: I'd ask the union rep for a written **job-cuts agreement** before any system goes live.
I'd finally attend Calder's **training** so I can judge what the software really does.
I'd keep **eight months** of costs in a safe account and delay buying a flat.
feel: I feel **annoyed** at having to learn what I don't trust, with a small stubborn pride underneath.
S1.quote: I'd rather make my own mistakes where I can see them.
fieldNote: She is **resistant** but pragmatic enough to go to training once the threat is concrete.
Her main concern is **Priya**, a junior colleague, not herself; guilt shapes her answer.
Her instinct is **collective**: union agreement first, personal adaptation second.

steps.text: Ask the union rep for a written job-cuts agreement
Attend Calder's buying-software training this spring
Keep eight months of costs in a safe account
Hold off on buying a flat for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say two years is far too fast and that governments must act immediately: a pay fund, retraining, and a limit on firing people for software. I'd say it loudly at work, because I think quiet people get steamrolled. Online I'd back any campaign calling for rules before rollout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job is mostly gone within a couple of years. Everything I do at the desk is the thing the card says AI does as well or better and cheaper. Robots aren't a worry for my kind of work, since I'm not lifting boxes, but that doesn't help me. Care homes still need gloves, so the company might survive, but not with me buying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move my savings to a very safe place and cut my spending hard, so my eight months become twelve or more. I'd talk with Dev about moving closer to the hospital, since nursing is hands-on and would last a few years longer. I'd look for a job that deals with people or with the supply chain on the ground, like managing the warehouse, and I'd use the union to demand redundancy terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, I'll say it plainly. It would feel like the floor going out from under a life I built carefully, and I'd be angry that those making the money get to decide the timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. What would you do in the very first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call a meeting with our union rep and the other buyers that same week, and ask Calder for a written plan. Then I'd sit down with Dev and a spreadsheet and work out how long we can live on one nurse's pay. Boring things first, because they're what keeps panic away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider using the AI tools yourself to stay ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's what everyone would tell me to do, and part of me knows they're right. But if AI can do my job cheaper, learning to press its buttons doesn't protect me. I'd rather use the time to move toward work that involves people in the room.

say: I'd say two years is **far too fast** and governments must act now.
I'd demand a pay **fund** and retraining before firms replace staff.
I'd speak up loudly at work, because quiet people get **steamrolled**.
think: My buying job is **mostly gone** within a couple of years, since it's all desk work.
Robots don't threaten me directly, but **that doesn't help**, because the thinking part goes first.
do: I'd cut spending so **eight months** of savings stretch to twelve or more.
I'd plan with Dev a possible **move** near the hospital where Dev works.
I'd push the union for **redundancy terms** and look at warehouse or people-facing roles.
feel: I feel **frightened** and angry that those profiting set the **timetable**.
S2.quote: If AI can do my job cheaper, learning to press its buttons doesn't protect me.
fieldNote: She expects her whole role to go; her answers are **plain and practical**, not dramatic.
She rejects learning AI as a **false fix**, which is consistent with her resistance.
Dev's nursing job is her **hedge**: the household has one hands-on earner.

steps.text: Cut spending so savings last twelve months or more
Move savings to a very safe account
Call a meeting of buyers and the union rep within a week
Apply for warehouse management or people-facing supply roles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us a real chance, but only if we use it, so I'd be pushing hard for a legal framework early. At work I'd ask Calder to publish a plan for the buying team. Among friends I'd say don't panic, but don't pretend it's nothing either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years feels like enough time to adjust but not enough to relax. I'd still lose the buying role at some point, so the question is where I'd end up. The thing in my favour is that I'm twenty-seven, have a master's degree, and money behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year trying to get the company to commit to something. I'd also do a part-time course in healthcare management, evenings, because care homes will always need people who understand them. I'd keep my spending flat, put the rest into savings, and keep the flat purchase on ice until I know where I'll work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More hopeful than the two-year one, but with a nagging edge. Five years is long enough to hear the clock ticking every time a new system gets switched on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a course. Why healthcare management and not something in technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I trust what I've seen. Dev tells me about the ward, and I know the gaps in what care homes get from suppliers. I'd rather build on what I understand, with people I respect, than chase a field I'd always feel behind in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the company need to do in those five years to earn your trust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Give us dates and numbers. If Calder says the buying team will shrink by two over three years and offers retraining on full pay, I can work with that. What I can't stand is being told everything's fine until the day a meeting invite shows up.

say: I'd say five years is a **real chance** if we use it to build a legal framework.
I'd ask Calder to **publish a plan** for the buying team.
I'd tell friends not to panic, but also **not to pretend** it's nothing.
think: Five years is enough to adjust but not to **relax**, and I'd still lose the buying role eventually.
I'm 27 with a master's and **savings**, so I should land somewhere decent.
do: I'd start an evening **healthcare management course** in the first year.
I'd keep spending flat and put the rest into **savings**.
I'd keep the **flat purchase** on hold until I know where I'll work.
feel: I feel **cautiously hopeful** with a nagging sense of a ticking clock.
S3.quote: What I can't stand is being told everything's fine until the day a meeting invite shows up.
fieldNote: She uses the **time** to retrain toward what she already knows: care and supply.
Trust in her employer hinges on **transparency**, a theme from her union leanings.
The home purchase is a quiet **casualty** of uncertainty.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening healthcare management course this autumn
Save every pound above current spending
Ask Calder to publish dates for the buying team
Put off the flat purchase until the job picture is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds almost manageable, so I'd say it's a chance to get the rules right. I'd tell people at work to treat it like a long project with milestones, and I'd argue for public retraining funds now. Online I'd push for politicians to commit to a timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel uneasy but not threatened. A decade is long, and by then I'll be 37 and could easily have moved into management, ethics of sourcing, or healthcare. The risk is complacency, since ten years lets people put their head in the sand, and I'm someone who might.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, keep saving, and maybe finally buy the flat, since a decade is long enough to own it. I'd start learning one AI tool properly, slowly, so I'm not frightened by it. I'd also join the union's working group on technology, so I'm helping set the terms from the start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly relaxed, with some curiosity. If ten years is real, I could even enjoy the early stages, as long as nobody is lying to me about the end point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years could make you complacent. How would you stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put reminders in my calendar, honestly. Every January I'd check what's changed at work, what skills the supplier reps are asking for, and what Dev's hospital is doing. A yearly check is small enough to do and big enough to matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change anything about family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably. Dev and I have talked about children around thirty-one. With a decade of warning and savings, I'd go ahead, but I'd want us both in jobs that robots reach last, so one of us is always secure.

say: I'd say ten years is a chance to **get the rules right**.
I'd tell colleagues to treat this like a long project with **milestones**.
I'd push politicians for a public **retraining** fund and a timetable.
think: I feel **uneasy** but not threatened, since by 37 I could be in management or healthcare.
My real risk is **complacency**, because ten years lets me avoid the subject.
do: I'd finally **buy the flat**, because a decade is long enough to own it.
I'd learn **one AI tool** properly and slowly, so it stops frightening me.
I'd join the union's **technology working group** to help set terms.
feel: I feel **fairly relaxed** with some curiosity, as long as nobody lies about the end point.
S4.quote: A yearly check is small enough to do and big enough to matter.
fieldNote: With time, her resistance **softens**: she plans to learn one tool slowly.
Family planning (children around **31**) is the clearest link between the scenario and her life.
She names her own **complacency** as the risk.

steps.text: Buy the flat once the buying team's future looks clear
Learn one AI buying tool slowly over the first year
Join the union's technology working group
Go ahead with children around thirty-one, with both jobs hands-on-safe

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because two years isn't enough for a country to agree on anything, never mind a care sector that runs on thin budgets. What would help is a rule that companies have to keep people on, or pay properly into a fund, when they swap a team for software. And I'd want the union at Calder to have a seat when management decides which jobs go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much I rely on people I trust rather than numbers. Everyone keeps telling me software can compare prices better than I can, and maybe it can, but it can't ring me at ten at night to say a delivery is going to be late. I'd like someone to ask whether that counts for anything.

headlineQuote: I see where our products end up, and that keeps the job feeling real to me.
portrait: Tara is a 27-year-old senior buyer at a care-supplies distributor, who keeps a **paper notebook** of every supplier rep's number.
She leans left, favours **unions** and regulation, and never uses AI tools, which she distrusts after a colleague's costly forecast.
She stays calm in the plateau world, but turns **anxious** once buying is named, worrying most about her junior colleague Priya.
Her instinct is collective: **union agreements** first, personal adaptation second.
Dev, her partner, is a nurse; that hands-on job is the household's **hedge** and anchors her plans.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries her most, since two years is too short for governments or care-sector budgets to adapt.
whatWouldHelp: A legal rule that firms keep people on or pay into a **fund** when replacing teams.
A **union seat** at Calder when management decides which jobs go.
